title: Wolves & Finance vs. TPUSA: Checking the Claims Against the Actual IRS Filings
summary: An assessment of the Wolves & Finance TPUSA investigation, checked where it is checkable — against the actual Form 990 filings rather than against coverage of the dispute. The core factual claim holds up: 1Ten LLC did receive substantial payments from a Turning Point entity. Several framings around it do not survive contact with the returns. This entry also keeps the financial thread separate from the Candace Owens / Mitch Snow Fort Huachuca allegation, which is unrelated to it and is now federal litigation.
sources_quality: A for the financial findings — read directly from IRS Form 990 e-file renderings (Turning Point USA Inc, EIN 80-0835023; Turning Point Action Inc, EIN 46-4331510), FEC Schedule B records via the Commission's API, and Arizona Secretary of State campaign finance report PDFs. All three are primary government records. Arizona coverage is partial: individual report PDFs are directly retrievable but the portal's search API could not be driven programmatically, so state-level totals here are a floor, not a complete accounting.
last_updated: August 2026 (IRS + FEC + Arizona state filings; split-dollar trend added)
key_takeaway: Checked against IRS, FEC and Arizona state records, the underlying financial claim holds up better the further the checking goes, while the entity-level framing remains wrong. Identified payments to 1Ten LLC now total approximately $3.61 million from Turning Point entities — $2.42 million on Turning Point Action's Form 990 contractor schedules plus $1.19 million from Turning Point PAC in FEC filings — with roughly $4.06 million across all payers and all three record systems, and the Arizona layer is only partially counted. The circulating $4.7 million figure is therefore closer to a floor than an exaggeration. Two corrections to this app's earlier passes matter. The “Suite 105-503” mailbox detail is real: it appears in Arizona Secretary of State filings, though not in the IRS returns, and an earlier version of this entry wrongly marked it refuted after checking only the federal documents. And the two official record systems give different street numbers for the same vendor, 18521 versus 18251. What has not changed: none of this money comes from the 501(c)(3) charity, whose returns contain no payments to 1Ten at all; none of it is concealed, the vendor being named across four consecutive IRS returns, 86 itemised FEC records and state reports; the service descriptions are specific and consistent throughout; and the vendor bills a diversified client book. The documented insider threads remain the ones nobody is arguing about — TPUSA CFO Justin Olson's own Senate campaign paid this vendor, and TPUSA's Schedule L discloses a split-dollar life insurance loan with an entity owned by Charlie Kirk.

findings.claim: 1Ten LLC received substantial payments from a Turning Point entity
findings.detail: Confirmed directly in the IRS filings. 1TEN LLC, 18521 E Queen Creek Rd, Queen Creek, AZ 85142, appears in Part VII Section B (five highest compensated independent contractors) of Turning Point Action Inc's Form 990 for four consecutive years, described each time as “social/digital media/ad placement”: $128,000 in TY2021, $721,573 in TY2022 (second-highest contractor that year), $469,105 in TY2023, and $1,100,998 in TY2024 (highest-paid contractor that year). Total across those four returns: approximately $2.42 million. It does not appear in the TY2020 top-five. The underlying factual claim that large sums went to this company is correct and independently verifiable by anyone.

findings.claim: The payments came from the 501(c)(3) charity, Turning Point USA Inc
findings.detail: They did not. Every disclosure located is in Turning Point Action Inc, EIN 46-4331510, a 501(c)(4) social welfare organization — the political advocacy arm. The string “1Ten” does not appear anywhere in Turning Point USA Inc's TY2023 Form 990 (EIN 80-0835023). That charity's five highest-paid contractors that year were Resource One ($6,146,883, printing/publication), Mosaic Event Productions ($3,636,329, event audio and video), Active Engagement ($2,659,870, digital education and fundraising), American Solutions for Business ($2,026,589, printing) and Conrad Direct ($1,144,800, mailing list rental). The distinction matters: a (c)(4) may lawfully engage in substantial political activity that a (c)(3) may not, and ad placement is an ordinary (c)(4) expense. Framing these payments as tax-deductible donor dollars leaving a charity misdescribes which entity paid.

findings.claim: The payments were hidden or concealed from public view
findings.detail: The opposite is closer to true as a matter of disclosure mechanics. Part VII Section B requires naming only the five highest-compensated contractors above $100,000, and 1Ten LLC is named there in four straight years, with address and service description, on returns that are public by law and freely readable. Turning Point Action reported only 7 contractors above $100,000 in TY2022, so the top-five list captures nearly all of its significant vendors. Whatever questions remain about the payments, they were reported where the IRS requires them to be reported. Note that this cuts the other way for any year a vendor falls outside the top five, where no naming is required — which is a limit of the form, not evidence of concealment.

findings.claim: The filings list a UPS Store mailbox suite as 1Ten LLC's address
findings.detail: CORRECTION. An earlier version of this entry marked this refuted, on the basis that the IRS Form 990 filings give 1Ten LLC a bare street address with no suite or box number. That was accurate about the federal nonprofit returns but wrong as a general statement, and the error was one of over-generalising from one document set to “the filings.” Arizona Secretary of State campaign finance records do carry the suite designation: the Republican Party of Arizona's 2022 Post-General (Q4) report lists the payee as 1Ten at “18251 E Queen Creek Rd, STE 105-503, Queen Creek, AZ 85142.” The “Suite 105-503” detail that features in the shell-company framing is therefore real and appears in a primary public filing. Renting a mailbox remains lawful and ordinary for small or remote firms, so this establishes the factual detail, not an inference from it.

findings.claim: The address 1Ten LLC reports is consistent between federal and state filings
findings.detail: It is not, and the discrepancy is in the street number itself. Turning Point Action's IRS Form 990 returns give “18521 E QUEEN CREEK RD” across four consecutive years. The Arizona Secretary of State filing gives “18251 E Queen Creek Rd, STE 105-503.” Those are transposed digits — 18521 versus 18251 — so at least one filing set carries an incorrect address for the same vendor, and the federal returns additionally omit the suite. Transposition is an obvious and unremarkable clerical error, and nothing here indicates intent. It is recorded because address consistency is the specific thing the shell-company claim turns on, and no party appears to have noticed that the two official records disagree.

findings.claim: The filings disclose 1Ten LLC as a related party or insider transaction
findings.detail: They do not, and this is the crux of the dispute rather than a resolution of it. 1Ten is reported as an arms-length independent contractor, not on Schedule L. The name “Hoffman” does not appear anywhere in Turning Point Action's TY2022 return, so no officer, director, trustee or key employee of that entity is disclosed by that name. Reporting attributes ownership of 1Ten LLC to Arizona state senator Jake Hoffman, a former TPUSA communications director, sourced to his own state financial disclosure forms rather than to the 990s. If that ownership is accurate, whether the payments required Schedule L disclosure turns on whether he met the tax definition of an interested person for the paying entity — a communications director is not automatically an officer, key employee or trustee for Form 990 purposes. This app has not verified the ownership and takes no position on whether the reporting treatment was correct.

findings.claim: TPUSA Inc's own filings disclose a related-party transaction involving Charlie Kirk personally
findings.detail: This is the most substantive related-party item located, and it is in the charity's own Schedule L for TY2023 — self-reported, not alleged. Part II (Loans to and/or From Interested Persons) lists GGLF 2023 LLC, described as an “entity owned by president/CEO,” for a “split dollar life insurance policy”: original principal $350,000, balance due $355,268, not in default, approved by the board or a committee, with a written agreement in place. Split-dollar life insurance arrangements between nonprofits and executives are a known, lawful and legitimately scrutinized compensation technique, and the reported governance safeguards — board approval and a written agreement — are the ones a reviewer would want to see present. Nothing here indicates wrongdoing. It is recorded because it is the actual disclosed insider transaction in these filings, and it has gone essentially unmentioned while attention focused on a vendor in a different entity.

findings.claim: The split-dollar life insurance arrangement with Charlie Kirk's LLC doubled in the fiscal year before his death
findings.detail: Comparing consecutive Schedule L filings: for TY2023 the GGLF 2023 LLC arrangement is reported at $350,000 original principal with a $355,268 balance due. For TY2024 — the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025 — it is reported at $700,000 original principal with a $735,737 balance. The arrangement doubled in the last full fiscal year before Kirk's death on September 10, 2025. Both years report board or committee approval, a written agreement, and no default. This is recorded because it is a documented change in a disclosed insider transaction and belongs in the record. It does not support an inference of foreknowledge and should not be read as one: TPUSA's revenue grew from roughly $85 million to $115.5 million across the same period, and scaling key-person coverage alongside a 36 percent revenue increase is ordinary practice for an organisation of that size. The increase also occurred at some point within a fiscal year that closed more than two months before the shooting, with no public evidence fixing it nearer. Split-dollar arrangements are a standard, lawful executive retention and estate-planning tool.

findings.claim: The disposition of the policy following Kirk's death is publicly known
findings.detail: It is not yet knowable from filings, and the reason is purely calendrical. TPUSA's fiscal year ends June 30, so Kirk's death on September 10, 2025 falls in fiscal year 2026. The TY2024 return covering the year ending June 2025 was filed May 15, 2026 and is the most recent available. The return covering the death — which would show whether the split-dollar loan was repaid, forgiven, settled from policy proceeds, or restructured, and how any death benefit was allocated between the organisation, the estate and the LLC — is not due until roughly May 2027. Who the beneficiary was under the arrangement is also not disclosed in the filings reviewed. This is a defined, dated, answerable question with a known future disclosure point, which is unusual in this case and worth flagging as a standing item rather than a mystery.

findings.claim: TPUSA Inc's TY2023 filing discloses excess benefit transactions or insider business dealings
findings.detail: Schedule L Part I (Excess Benefit Transactions), Part III (Grants or Assistance Benefiting Interested Persons) and Part IV (Business Transactions Involving Interested Persons) are all blank on the TY2023 return. The organization also answers “Yes” to having a written conflict of interest policy with annual disclosure and regular monitoring and enforcement, a written whistleblower policy, a written document retention and destruction policy, and compensation review using independent persons and comparability data. These are self-reported answers on a self-prepared return and are not audit findings, but a claim that the filings themselves show self-dealing by the charity is not supported by what the filings say.

findings.claim: The reported cumulative figure of roughly $4.7 million to 1Ten is verified
findings.detail: UPDATED after querying FEC records. An earlier pass of this entry logged this as not established, having checked only IRS filings. Adding Federal Election Commission Schedule B disbursement data substantially closes the gap. FEC records show $1,551,021.22 disbursed to 1Ten LLC across all federal committees, of which $1,190,589.39 came from TURNING POINT PAC INC. (committee C00814152) across 52 payments in 2022, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Combined with the $2,418,676 disclosed in Turning Point Action's Form 990 contractor schedules for TY2021-TY2024, total identified payments from Turning Point entities come to approximately $3.61 million, and approximately $3.97 million including all federal payers. The circulating figure of roughly $4.7 million is therefore in the right range rather than inflated, and the remaining difference is readily explained: a large share of the FEC purpose codes are marked “NON-FED,” meaning non-federal state and local activity that is reported to state authorities rather than the FEC, and Turning Point Action's TY2020 and TY2025 returns plus any year the vendor fell outside the top-five naming threshold would add more.

findings.claim: The filings establish whether the payments were reasonable value for services rendered
findings.detail: They cannot, and this is the honest limit of documents-based analysis. A Form 990 records that an amount was paid, to whom, and for what broad category of service. It does not record deliverables, hours, market rates, competing bids, or whether the work was performed. Roughly $2.42 million for social and digital media and ad placement over four years is not on its face implausible for an organization whose revenue grew from $2.6 million to $37.5 million across a comparable period, and ad placement in particular is a pass-through-heavy category where the contractor's fee may be a fraction of the total. Establishing whether value was received would require records no public filing contains. Neither the accusation nor the defence can be settled from these documents.

findings.claim: Wolves & Finance is a documented channel with a verifiable author and stated method
findings.detail: The channel is run by Zach De Gregorio, who describes himself as an independent accountant based in Phoenix, Arizona, with an active CPA license and prior experience including a chief financial officer role, posting financial videos since 2015 under the framing that he follows the money through public records. His stated method on the TPUSA material is review of publicly filed IRS returns, and he states he is not working from leaks or inside sources. This is a materially better-sourced starting position than most independent commentary this app has assessed in this case.

findings.claim: TPUSA sent Wolves & Finance a cease-and-desist over the investigation
findings.detail: Reported in January 2026. Coverage indicates one specific point of contention was De Gregorio's use of the word “audit” to characterize his review, which TPUSA's counsel objected to. TPUSA has separately rejected the underlying claims and characterized them as conspiracy theories while urging supporters to stay focused on the organization's mission. A cease-and-desist is a private legal demand, not a court finding, and establishes nothing about whether the underlying analysis is right or wrong — it establishes only that the organization moved to stop the publication.

findings.claim: Wolves & Finance originated the Mitch Snow / Fort Huachuca eyewitness allegation
findings.detail: The eyewitness allegation originates with Mitch Snow and was amplified by Candace Owens, who brought him on her programme; it does not originate with this channel. PARTIAL CORRECTION (August 2026): an earlier version of this finding went further and characterised the channel's Kirk-case output as confined to case analysis and TPUSA financial work, on the basis of its published video listing. That was too strong. De Gregorio has separately advanced Fort Huachuca material of his own — reportedly arguing that the installation, home to the U.S. Army Intelligence Center of Excellence, received repurposed federal funding and theorising that money appropriated for southern border security was diverted toward the killing. That is a substantially more speculative claim than his documents-based nonprofit-finance work, it rests on a different and weaker evidentiary footing, and this app has verified neither the funding premise nor the diversion theory. The distinction that survives is one of origin and method, not of subject matter: he did not originate the eyewitness claim, but he is not confined to filings analysis either, and the two strands of his output should be weighted separately rather than inheriting each other's credibility.

findings.claim: The Fort Huachuca planning allegation is now the subject of federal litigation
findings.detail: Brian Harpole, head of security for Kirk's American Comeback Tour, filed a federal defamation suit on April 30, 2026 against Candace Owens, her companies, and Mitchell Snow. The complaint alleges they falsely tied him to a plot to kill Kirk and broadcast it across social media and Owens' show, specifically the claim that he secretly met with Army intelligence officers at Fort Huachuca the day before the killing — which Harpole characterizes as “completely and obviously fabricated.” He asserts he was in Dallas, Texas at the time and that travel records support that. Causes of action include defamation, false light invasion of privacy, and civil conspiracy to defame; the complaint seeks damages exceeding $75,000 and an injunction requiring removal of the statements. A filed complaint is an allegation, not an adjudication, and the case appears to remain in early stages.

findings.claim: The video content itself could be reviewed for this entry
findings.detail: It could not. YouTube video transcripts, descriptions, and on-screen exhibits are not retrievable through the tools available to this app — a limitation encountered consistently across every video-based claim assessed in this case, including the ballistics channels. Everything above rests on the channel's own website, secondary written coverage, and court filings. Any specific documentary exhibit shown on-screen in those videos has therefore not been examined here, and no claim in this entry should be read as an assessment of evidence displayed in them.

findings.claim: A third Turning Point entity, not previously identified in this entry, is the largest federal payer
findings.detail: TURNING POINT PAC INC., FEC committee ID C00814152, is a separate entity from both Turning Point USA Inc (the 501(c)(3)) and Turning Point Action Inc (the 501(c)(4)). It disbursed $1,190,589.39 to 1Ten LLC across 52 separate payments. The money is therefore spread across at least two Turning Point entities plus their affiliated committee structure, which is a large part of why totals compiled from any single source come out low. Payments continued well past Charlie Kirk's death: $524,256.81 in calendar 2025 and $120,180.92 in calendar 2026 to date, against $830,962.13 in 2022 and $75,621.36 in 2024.

findings.claim: The FEC purpose codes describe a coherent and specific service, not vague consulting
findings.detail: Across 86 de-duplicated disbursement records the descriptions are consistent and concrete, overwhelmingly text-messaging and print work: “non-fed text services” (31 records), “texting” (8), “non-federal text messaging” (7), “non-fed printing” (7), plus digital media, slate-piece get-out-the-vote mailers naming specific Arizona candidates, and prepayments for text services. This matters to the assessment in both directions. Vague “consulting” line items with no deliverable are a classic red flag; itemized SMS and print work with named candidate slates is the opposite pattern, and it matches the “social/digital media/ad placement” description on the Form 990s. It remains true that a purpose code records what a committee said it bought, not what was delivered.

findings.claim: 1Ten LLC exists solely as a vehicle for Turning Point money
findings.detail: The FEC record shows a diversified client book, which is meaningful evidence against the shell-company framing. Beyond Turning Point PAC, 1Ten LLC received $300,680.71 from the REPUBLICAN PARTY OF ARIZONA (C00008227) across 9 payments in 2022, $40,340.54 from MOMS FOR LIBERTY ACTION (C00791848) across 22 payments in 2024-2026, and smaller sums from three individual candidate committees. A company invoicing a state party committee, a national advocacy organization and multiple campaigns over several cycles, in itemized amounts, for a consistent service line, is behaving like an operating vendor rather than a conduit built around one client. This does not resolve whether any particular payment was appropriate, but the specific accusation that the entity exists only to move Turning Point funds is not supported by the record.

findings.claim: A TPUSA officer's own campaign committee paid the same vendor
findings.detail: Newly identified here and not found in any coverage reviewed. FEC records show JUSTIN OLSON FOR U.S. SENATE (committee C00791467) disbursed $10,920.44 to 1Ten LLC in 2022. Justin Olson has served as Chief Financial Officer of Turning Point USA since December 2019 and is listed among the organization's officers on its Form 990; he is also a former Arizona state representative and Corporation Commissioner, and ran in the 2022 Republican primary for U.S. Senate in Arizona, losing to Blake Masters — whose committee separately paid 1Ten LLC $7,617.50. The dollar figure is small and a candidate hiring an established Arizona political vendor is unremarkable in isolation. It is recorded because it documents a direct interlock between the vendor and a named financial officer of the charity at the centre of the dispute, which is the kind of relationship a related-party analysis turns on and which no reporting located has mentioned.

findings.claim: Arizona state filings contain further payments to 1Ten beyond the IRS and FEC records
findings.detail: Confirmed, and this is where the previously unaccounted money begins to appear. The Republican Party of Arizona's 2022 Post-General (Q4) report to the Arizona Secretary of State records payments to 1Ten under the category “Communications - Advertising,” including a $75,000.00 entry dated 11/02/2022 and a further $14,957.88 entry in mid-November 2022 — on the order of $90,000 within this single quarterly report from a single committee. These are state-account payments, reported to Arizona rather than the FEC, and are therefore additional to the $300,680.71 the same party committee disbursed through its federal account. This directly corroborates the inference drawn earlier from the “NON-FED” purpose codes in the FEC data: there is a real state-level layer to these payments.

findings.claim: This app has produced a complete accounting of payments to 1Ten LLC
findings.detail: It has not, and the remaining gap is now well characterised rather than mysterious. Arizona's See The Money portal serves individual report PDFs at stable public URLs, which are directly retrievable and machine readable, but the portal's vendor-search API could not be driven programmatically from this environment and the interactive site sits behind a bot challenge that this app will not attempt to circumvent. Report URLs use opaque GUIDs that cannot be enumerated, so reports must be located individually. What is documented here is one quarterly report from one committee. A full state accounting would require every quarterly filing from every Arizona committee that used this vendor across 2021-2026, which is achievable by anyone with portal access and is the obvious next step for a serious audit.

fact_check_gap: Three public record systems hold pieces of this story and no coverage located has consulted more than one. The IRS returns show which entity paid and that the charity did not; the FEC shows a third Turning Point entity is the largest federal payer and that the vendor has a diversified client book; the Arizona filings hold the mailbox suite number that the shell-company framing rests on, plus a further payment layer, plus an address that does not match the federal record. Anyone can retrieve all three. The Arizona report PDFs in particular are served at stable public URLs and are the least-examined and most probative of the remaining sources.

title: Daily Wire Ownership and the Aircraft Question
summary: Who actually controls The Daily Wire, who its outside shareholders are, what aircraft those people are reported to operate, and whether any of it appears in this app's transponder record for the day Charlie Kirk was killed. The ownership picture is well documented. The aircraft answer is a clean negative.
sources_quality: B+ for the ownership structure (consistent across multiple business-press summaries, and the Wilks seed investment is already corroborated in this app's network research); A for the negative aircraft finding, which was run against this app's own extraction of the adsb.lol archive for 2025-09-10; C for the reported Wilks aircraft types, which could not be confirmed against the FAA registry directly.
key_takeaway: The Daily Wire's board is tightly held by three people — co-CEOs Jeremy Boreing and Caleb Robinson and co-founder Ben Shapiro — operating through Bentkey Ventures LLC, formerly Forward Publishing LLC. The meaningful outside stakes are family: Farris Wilks at roughly 15 percent, Levi Wilks at about 7 percent, and Dennis Prager at about 3 percent, with the company valued in the $600-800 million range by early 2026. Farris Wilks seeded the company with about $4.7 million in 2015, a fact this app's network research already documents. On aircraft: the Wilks family is reported to operate a Gulfstream G650ER and a Bombardier Global Express, though this app could not confirm tail numbers against the FAA registry. Regardless, the case-relevant test returns nothing. No aircraft linked to the Wilks family, Bentkey Ventures, Forward Publishing, or any Daily Wire principal appears anywhere in this app's catalogued transponder data for Utah or the Provo area on September 10, 2025.

findings.claim: The Daily Wire's board is controlled by its founders rather than outside investors
findings.detail: Reporting consistently describes the board as tightly held by co-CEO Jeremy Boreing, co-founder Ben Shapiro, and co-CEO Caleb Robinson, with the business operating as Bentkey Ventures LLC (previously Forward Publishing LLC). Outside stakes are minority and concentrated in one family plus one longtime ally: Farris Wilks around 15 percent, Levi Wilks around 7 percent, Dennis Prager around 3 percent. As a privately held company The Daily Wire does not file the public ownership disclosures that would let this be confirmed from primary documents, so this rests on business-press reporting rather than filings.

findings.claim: The Wilks family's role in The Daily Wire is already established in this app's research
findings.detail: Yes, and it is not new. This app's network dataset already records that Shapiro left the David Horowitz Freedom Center in 2015 and, with Jeremy Boreing, founded The Daily Wire on roughly $4.7 million in initial financing from Farris Wilks. That entry also expressly notes the seed money came principally from the Wilks family rather than from Robert Shillman, correcting a conflation that circulates elsewhere. The app separately records that after Kirk's death Shapiro announced The Daily Wire would donate $1 million to TPUSA.

findings.claim: Specific aircraft owned by Daily Wire principals or the Wilks family could be identified from the FAA registry
findings.detail: Not by this app. Secondary sources report the Wilks family operates a Gulfstream G650ER and a Bombardier Global Express, but no tail number is given, and direct queries to the FAA aircraft registry by owner name (“Wilks,” “Bentkey,” “Forward Publishing”) did not return usable results through available tools. Business aircraft are also routinely registered to holding LLCs or trustee entities whose names bear no relation to the beneficial owner, which is lawful and extremely common — this app's own Provo dataset is full of such registrations. So an owner-name search is a weak instrument here even when it works, and absence of a name match is not absence of an aircraft.

findings.claim: An aircraft linked to The Daily Wire or the Wilks family was present near Provo on September 10, 2025
findings.detail: No such aircraft appears in this app's catalogued transponder data. The scan covered the Provo-area and Utah aircraft extracted from the adsb.lol historical archive for 2025-09-10 against the strings Wilks, Bentkey, Forward, Daily, Shapiro, Boreing, Prager and Frac, returning zero matches. None of the 18 private jets catalogued around Provo that day carries an owner of record connected to any of these parties. This is the same method previously applied to the Adelson tail-number theory, which also returned zero matches across the archive.

findings.claim: The Global Express in the Provo data could be a Wilks aircraft
findings.detail: Worth checking because the Wilks family is reported to operate that airframe type, but it does not hold. The only Global Express-family aircraft in the Provo dataset is N1098L, a Global 6000/6500 registered to LASAI AVIATION II LLC, which this app has already examined in detail. That entry records no documented tie between Lasai Aviation II LLC and any case figure, and the aircraft's own broadcast position places it at 42.287 N, -112.4276 W at 12:22 PM MDT — southeastern Idaho, roughly 144 miles from the UVU campus, at 30,000 feet in a climbing transit. It was not near Provo when Kirk was shot.

findings.claim: Aircraft ownership by media-company shareholders bears on the Kirk case
findings.detail: No connection has been established, and this app's prior aviation work is the relevant precedent. Its standing finding is that no military, ISR, or flagged civilian aircraft has been tied to anyone in Kirk's circle. The aircraft that drew the most early attention, N888KG, was publicly ruled out by FBI Director Kash Patel on September 21, 2025, and this app separately found the widely circulated flight narrative about it contradicted by the primary archive, including a stated shooting time about two hours off (contradiction X12). Wealthy political donors owning private jets is a base-rate observation, not evidence; establishing relevance would require a specific aircraft in a specific place at a specific time, which is exactly the test run above and failed.

fact_check_gap: Aircraft-ownership questions in this case have consistently been raised in the abstract — who owns a jet — rather than in the falsifiable form that actually settles them: did a named tail number broadcast a position near Provo on September 10, 2025. The archive needed to answer that is open, licensed for redistribution, and has been available since the day of the shooting.

title: The Medical Response Chain: Private Transport, the Two-Hour Gap, and the Wrong Hospital
summary: The emergency-response sequence between the shot and the death pronouncement had never been examined in this app. It turns out to contain one genuinely unusual operational fact, a two-hour-plus interval that has never been documented in detail, and a hospital detail that quietly resolves the direction of one of this app's open threads.
sources_quality: B+ for the transport method and pronouncement time (multiple contemporaneous outlets, plus a named eyewitness account from Frank Turek); B for the absence findings, which rest on the non-appearance of records rather than on any denial
key_takeaway: Kirk was not transported by ambulance. His own private security detail moved him in a private vehicle to Timpanogos Regional Hospital in Orem, with TPUSA's Frank Turek describing a journey made with the vehicle door open. He was pronounced dead at 2:40 p.m., roughly two hours and seventeen minutes after the 12:23 p.m. shot. Nothing about private transport is inherently improper — a protective detail moving a principal immediately rather than waiting for EMS is a recognised protective-medicine decision, and at close range it can be faster. But it means the best-documented minutes of the entire incident, the ones between wounding and hospital arrival, have no EMS run sheet, no paramedic observations, and no independent clinical record. Separately, the hospital detail resolves something: the unidentified man in this app's contradiction X39 was asking after Kirk at Intermountain Health Utah Valley Hospital, which is not where Kirk was taken. A person with inside knowledge would have known the right building.

findings.claim: Kirk was transported to hospital by ambulance
findings.detail: He was moved by his own security detail in a private vehicle to Timpanogos Regional Hospital in Orem. TPUSA speaker Frank Turek, present at the event, described the vehicle travelling with its door open for the journey. This is a documented and defensible protective-detail decision — immediate self-evacuation can beat waiting for an ambulance, and is standard practice in executive protection for penetrating trauma. It is recorded here because it is a materially different response chain from the one most coverage implies, and because it determines what records exist.

findings.claim: A detailed clinical record of the resuscitation attempt is in the public domain
findings.detail: No operative note, resuscitation timeline, imaging, or detailed pronouncement record has been published beyond the bare time of death. Because transport was private rather than by EMS, there is also no ambulance run sheet, no paramedic assessment, and no independent set of clinical observations from the transport interval. Combined with this app's existing finding that the autopsy remains sealed and that Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Deirdre Amaro has never testified — the cause of death reaching the court only secondhand through investigator David Hull, over defence objection — the entire medical record of this case rests on documents no outside party has examined.

findings.claim: The interval between the shot and the death pronouncement is documented
findings.detail: Only its endpoints are. The shot was fired at approximately 12:23 p.m. and Kirk was pronounced dead at 2:40 p.m., an interval of roughly two hours and seventeen minutes. What happened within it — arrival time at Timpanogos Regional, what interventions were attempted, and when clinical death was determined as against when it was formally pronounced — is not in any source reviewed. A pronouncement time is an administrative act and does not necessarily coincide with the time of death, which is one reason the sealed autopsy matters more than usual here.

findings.claim: The unidentified man in X39 demonstrated inside knowledge of Kirk's location
findings.detail: The opposite, and this is the most useful single detail recovered in this pass. Unsealed warrants describe an unidentified man in a dark suit, sunglasses and a prosthetic arm who appeared at Intermountain Health Utah Valley Hospital asking about Kirk's whereabouts, conduct that reads as sinister in isolation. But Kirk was taken to Timpanogos Regional Hospital, a different facility. Asking after someone at the wrong hospital is the behaviour of a person trying to find out where he had been taken, not of a person with advance knowledge or operational involvement. This does not identify the man or explain why a warrant initially called him “the suspect in this case,” both of which remain open, but it materially weakens the most suspicious reading of his conduct.

timeline_sequence.event: Kirk shot at UVU amphitheatre
Private security detail moves Kirk in a private vehicle rather than awaiting EMS; Frank Turek describes the journey made with the door open
Arrival at Timpanogos Regional Hospital, Orem — arrival time not published in any source reviewed
Pronounced dead at Timpanogos Regional Hospital — roughly 2h17m after the shot
An unidentified man asks after Kirk at Intermountain Health Utah Valley Hospital — the wrong facility
Motorcade departs Timpanogos Regional with Kirk's body

fact_check_gap: The response chain has gone almost entirely unexamined despite being the one part of the incident with the most potential documentary trail. No outlet reviewed has asked why transport was private rather than by EMS, what the arrival time was, or what the two-hour interval contained. Nor has any coverage connected the hospital the unidentified man visited to the hospital Kirk was actually taken to, though both facts were separately public.

title: Prosecutorial Conduct, Venue, and Who Pays: The Procedural Record Nobody Catalogued
summary: Four procedural threads this app had never logged: a prosecutor held in civil contempt for violating the gag order, a denied change-of-venue bid argued by the expert from the Kohberger case, the taxpayer funding behind Robinson's capital defence team, and the immunity deal that kept Lance Twiggs from being charged.
sources_quality: A- — named parties, specific dates, and rulings from a named judge, reported consistently across KSL, Deseret News, ABC4, KUTV and CNN
key_takeaway: The most significant omission from this app's record until now: on June 26, 2026, Judge Tony Graf held Deputy Utah County Attorney Christopher Ballard in civil contempt for violating the court's gag order, over interviews given in March 2026 to TMZ, USA Today, PolitiFact and Fox News in which he characterised the strength of the state's case. The defence asked that the death penalty be struck as the sanction; Graf declined, holding that such a remedy would be grossly disproportionate to the misconduct and was not available within a civil contempt framework. So the prosecution has a formal judicial finding of misconduct against it, and the death penalty survived it. Alongside that: the change of venue was denied in favour of expanded questionnaires and larger jury pools, Robinson's defence is taxpayer-funded after a finding of indigency with Utah County approving over $1 million across both sides, and Lance Twiggs received limited use immunity from both state and federal prosecutors and has not been charged.

findings.claim: A prosecutor in this case has been formally sanctioned for misconduct
findings.detail: On June 26, 2026, Fourth District Judge Tony Graf found Deputy Utah County Attorney Christopher Ballard in civil contempt for violating the court's gag order. The conduct was a set of interviews given in March 2026 to TMZ, USA Today, PolitiFact and Fox News, in which Ballard commented publicly on the strength of the state's case. Ballard is already recorded in this app's case map as a member of the prosecution team. A civil contempt finding against a prosecutor in a capital case is a serious and unusual event, and it had not previously appeared anywhere in this app's record.

findings.claim: The contempt finding cost the state the death penalty
findings.detail: Defence counsel Richard Novak argued the appropriate remedy was to preclude the state from seeking death. Graf declined, ruling that striking the death penalty would be grossly disproportionate to the misconduct and was not a remedy legally available within the civil contempt framework he was applying. The death penalty accordingly remained on the table through this ruling — which is separate from, and earlier than, the August 2026 aggravator challenge already logged in this app as contradiction X36.

findings.claim: Robinson's defence is privately financed
findings.detail: It is publicly funded. Judge Graf found Robinson lacked the means to retain counsel, and the Utah County Commission contracted the defence team: Kathryn Nester of Salt Lake City as lead, with Michael Burt and Richard Novak of California as co-counsel, all experienced capital practitioners — Burt spent 24 years as head trial attorney at the San Francisco Public Defender's Office across a 47-year career, and Nester has 33 years and nine capital or aggravated murder cases behind her. Utah County approved over $1 million in taxpayer funding to support the proceedings on both sides. The composition of the team reflects an appointment system responding to a capital charge, not outside money, and the recurring suggestion that someone is quietly bankrolling the defence has no support.

findings.claim: The trial will be moved out of Utah County
findings.detail: The defence sought a change of venue and retained the same pretrial-publicity expert used in the Bryan Kohberger case, who testified on polling data, the demographics of the Utah County jury pool, and the way social media algorithms amplify local news coverage so that prospective jurors cannot easily avoid it. Judge Graf denied the motion, holding that less restrictive alternatives remained available: expanded juror questionnaires, larger jury pools, and extensive individual questioning during selection. Proceedings remain in Utah County before Judge Graf.

findings.claim: Lance Twiggs faced criminal exposure for his role
findings.detail: He was given limited use immunity by both the United States Attorney's Office and the Utah County Attorney's Office, and gave a recorded statement under oath on April 20, 2026, after an admonition that any false statement would be punishable and could itself be charged as obstruction. Use immunity means his statements cannot be used against him. No charges have been filed, and authorities have stated there is no indication he had prior knowledge of the assassination. The prosecution's decision not to charge the one person who indisputably knew before the surrender is itself informative about how the state reads the evidence of a wider circle: it does not appear to believe one exists.

findings.claim: The defence called no affirmative witnesses of its own
findings.detail: It called three, on DNA and ballistics, two of them from the ATF. Among them was ATF DNA Section Chief Caitlin Oliver, who testified that the analysis supported inclusion of Robinson's DNA while also addressing the limits of what such evidence can establish, stating that with forensic evidence it is impossible to state anything with total certainty. Robinson did not testify, on his attorneys' advice. The defence then rested, with briefing set for the September 1, 2026 oral arguments.

timeline_sequence.event: Judge Graf finds Robinson indigent; Utah County Commission contracts Nester, Burt and Novak; over $1 million approved across both sides
Deputy Utah County Attorney Christopher Ballard gives interviews to TMZ, USA Today, PolitiFact and Fox News commenting on the strength of the state's case
Defence presents pretrial-publicity expert from the Kohberger case on venue and jury-pool bias; motion later denied in favour of expanded questionnaires and larger pools
Lance Twiggs gives a recorded sworn statement under limited use immunity from both federal and county prosecutors
Defence argues the death penalty should be struck as sanction for the state's contempt
Graf holds Ballard in civil contempt but declines to strike the death penalty as grossly disproportionate and legally unavailable in that framework
Preliminary hearing; defence calls three witnesses on DNA and ballistics and rests; Robinson does not testify
Defence files the 41-page aggravator challenge (see contradiction X36)
Oral arguments scheduled on bindover and the death-penalty question

fact_check_gap: A prosecutor being held in contempt in a capital case is the kind of development that would ordinarily anchor coverage for a week, and it was reported once and largely dropped. It also cuts directly against a common framing of this case in both directions: it is evidence that the court is willing to sanction the state, and simultaneously evidence that the court will not convert a prosecutorial error into a windfall for the defence.

title: Harpole v. Owens and Snow: Separating Presence, Identification, and Alibi
summary: An evidentiary assessment of the Fort Huachuca dispute now that it is in federal court, asking specifically who the documented record supports. The answer is not the binary the public argument assumes. The evidence reasonably supports that Mitch Snow was at Fort Huachuca, and separately supports that Brian Harpole was in Dallas. Those are only contradictory if Snow correctly identified who he saw — and the person who amplified his account has now conceded that he may not have.
sources_quality: A- for the litigation record (federal docket, Harpole v. Owens et al, 3:26-cv-00556, M.D. Tenn.); B for the corroboration of Snow's presence, which rests on a document Candace Owens described publicly rather than one this app has examined, plus a hostile-source interview; C for the surrounding creator-ecosystem commentary, much of which is self-interested on both sides
key_takeaway: Three claims are being treated as one, and separating them resolves most of the dispute. First, was Snow at Fort Huachuca on September 9, 2025? The evidence reasonably supports yes, and notably the strongest corroboration came from an investigation trying to discredit him: Gary Melton interviewed Snow's estranged son, who said military police contacted him that day because he was listed as Snow's emergency contact. Owens has separately described an incident report with specific detail, including an officer taking Snow outside for questioning and bomb dogs called at 11:17 a.m. Second, was Harpole there? Harpole's complaint asserts travel records place him in Dallas, Texas, and the notable feature of Owens' response is that she does not appear to dispute the records exist — her counter is that they did not cover the window after the meeting ended, which is a timing argument, not a denial. Third, and decisively: Owens has publicly acknowledged that what could not be confirmed is Snow's memory of who he believed he saw, and that she remains open to the possibility those people were misidentified. That concession, from the claim's principal amplifier, is the single most important item in the record. It means the reconciling explanation — Snow was genuinely present, is possibly sincere, and misidentified the people he saw — fits every documented fact without requiring anyone to be lying.

findings.claim: Mitch Snow was physically at Fort Huachuca on September 9, 2025
findings.detail: Two independent-ish strands support this. Owens states she obtained an incident report and describes specific corroborating detail: Snow taken outside and questioned at length by a named captain, military police summoned, a possible bomb threat reported, and bomb dogs called at 11:17 a.m. More persuasively, the corroboration also came from a hostile source. Gary Melton, who ran an investigation explicitly aimed at discrediting Snow and interviewed his ex-wives and estranged son, produced an interview in which the son said he was contacted by military police on September 9 because he was listed as Snow's emergency contact. Evidence that emerges against the interest of the party developing it is generally the strongest kind. This app has not examined the incident report itself, so the finding is supported rather than verified.

findings.claim: Snow's presence at the base confirms that he saw Harpole or Erika Kirk there
findings.detail: It does not, and this conflation is the core analytical error running through the entire public dispute. Establishing that a person was at a location establishes nothing about the accuracy of who he says he observed there. Owens has framed the incident report as vindication of “Mitch's story,” but the report as she describes it goes to his presence and his detention, not to his identifications. The two questions require entirely different kinds of evidence: presence is documentary, identification is perceptual.

findings.claim: The person who amplified the claim has conceded the identification may be wrong
findings.detail: This is the most consequential item in the record and it has been almost entirely lost in the argument around it. Owens has publicly stated that what could not be confirmed was Snow's memory of who he believed he saw coming out of the early-morning meeting, and that she remains open to the possibility that the people he identified were misidentified. That is the claim's principal broadcaster acknowledging the specific element that names Harpole is unconfirmed and possibly mistaken. It does not retract the claim, and it may carry legal significance in a defamation action where a defendant's state of mind about truth or falsity is at issue, but that is for the court.

findings.claim: Harpole has produced evidence placing him elsewhere
findings.detail: His complaint asserts that travel records place him in Dallas, Texas, and characterises the Fort Huachuca allegation as completely and obviously fabricated. The significant detail is the shape of the response: reporting on the complaint indicates Owens had access to those travel records and dismissed them on the basis that they did not establish an alibi for the period after the alleged meeting concluded. That is an argument about the window the records cover, not an assertion that the records are forged or that Harpole was in Arizona. Neither side, on the current public record, appears to contend that the travel records do not exist or do not say what Harpole says they say. This app has not examined them; they are described in a pleading, which is an allegation, not a finding.

findings.claim: The dispute requires one of the two men to be lying
findings.detail: It does not, and this is the finding most at odds with how the dispute is discussed. A single explanation accommodates every documented fact: Snow was genuinely at Fort Huachuca, genuinely had an unusual and stressful encounter there involving military police, genuinely believes he saw people he recognised, and was mistaken about who they were. Harpole was in Dallas. Both accounts are then honestly held and one is simply wrong. Misidentification by a sincere witness under stress is among the most thoroughly documented phenomena in evidence law, and it is the ordinary explanation for exactly this pattern. It is also, notably, the possibility Owens herself has now allowed for. Sincerity would not necessarily defeat a defamation claim — republishing a false statement of fact can be actionable regardless of the original witness's good faith — but the truthfulness question the public argument is fixated on has a mundane answer available.

findings.claim: The litigation has reached any determination on the merits
findings.detail: It has not. Harpole v. Owens et al is docketed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee as 3:26-cv-00556, filed April 30, 2026, naming Owens, Candace Owens LLC, GeorgeTom Inc. and Mitchell Snow, and pleading defamation, false light, and civil conspiracy to defame with damages sought above $75,000 plus injunctive relief. Procedural developments to date: a federal judge authorised the U.S. Marshals Service to serve Snow in May 2026, the deadline for Owens to answer was extended by unopposed motion to August 6, 2026, Nashville attorney Daniel Horwitz appeared for Owens and her companies, and Harpole moved on an emergency basis for an evidence-preservation order referencing recent posts and a safety deposit box. No court has ruled on whether any statement was false or defamatory.

findings.claim: Requiring U.S. Marshals to serve a defendant is routine
findings.detail: Recorded because it is unusual enough to note without over-reading. Court-authorised Marshals Service service is a mechanism typically used when ordinary service has proven difficult, which can indicate evasion, an unlocatable defendant, or simply a plaintiff proceeding cautiously in a high-profile matter. This app has not located the underlying motion explaining why it was sought, so no inference is drawn about Snow's conduct. It is flagged as a documented procedural fact rather than as evidence of anything.

claim_variants.note: Four readings of the same dispute. Three of them are in active circulation; the fourth is this app's assessment. Separating presence from identification is what distinguishes them.

variants.assertion: Snow was never at Fort Huachuca and invented the entire account.
variants.source: Implicit in much of the debunking commentary
variants.status: NOT SUPPORTED — presence has independent corroboration, including from an investigation seeking to discredit him

variants.assertion: The incident report confirms Snow was at the base, therefore his identification of Harpole is confirmed.
variants.source: Candace Owens' framing of the incident report
variants.status: NON SEQUITUR — presence is documentary, identification is perceptual; the report speaks only to the former

variants.assertion: Harpole met Army intelligence officers at Fort Huachuca the day before the killing.
variants.source: Mitch Snow, amplified by Candace Owens
variants.status: NOT ESTABLISHED — contradicted by travel records described in the complaint, and conceded as possible misidentification by its own amplifier

variants.assertion: Snow was genuinely present, had a genuinely unusual encounter, and was mistaken about who he saw; Harpole was in Dallas.
variants.status: BEST FIT — accommodates every documented fact without requiring anyone to lie, and matches the possibility Owens herself now allows

fact_check_gap: The entire public argument has been conducted as a referendum on whether Mitch Snow is a liar, which is the wrong question and is answerable only in parts. Nobody appears to have separated the three distinct claims — presence, identification, and Harpole's whereabouts — or noticed that the strongest corroboration of Snow's presence came from the investigation trying to discredit him, or given weight to the amplifier's own concession that the identification may be mistaken. That concession is more probative than any of the surrounding commentary.

title: Lance Twiggs: The State's Most Important Witness, and the One Never Cross-Examined
summary: A focused assessment of Lance Twiggs — what his evidence establishes against Robinson, and what structurally weakens it. Nearly every incriminating item in this case passes through him: the note, the text thread, and the only reported verbal admission. He is also the one witness the defence was denied the chance to cross-examine, he testified under immunity from two prosecuting authorities, and his own DNA is on both key forensic exhibits.
sources_quality: A- for the procedural posture (rulings by a named judge, reported consistently by KSL, Fox 13, OANN and ABC4); B+ for the content of his recorded statement, which reaches this app through reporting on a video played in open court rather than through a transcript
key_takeaway: Twiggs is simultaneously the strongest evidence against Robinson and the state's largest procedural vulnerability. His account supplies the deception (Robinson leaving on September 10 claiming a long work shift), the note, the text thread containing operational detail that matches recovered physical evidence, the only reported verbal admission with expressed remorse, the bullet-engraving observation from 2025, and a statement that Robinson resembled the FBI wanted-poster image. He cooperated voluntarily and gave a DNA sample. Against that: the state entered his account as a recorded statement under Utah Rule 1102 rather than calling him live, the defence moved specifically to compel his appearance for cross-examination and was refused, and prosecutors argued he was “not material” to the preliminary hearing because the burden there is light. So the person whose conversations are the asserted basis for seeking the death penalty has never been cross-examined by anyone. The Confrontation Clause objection is preserved for trial, which means this is deferred rather than resolved — and reporting indicates he is no longer under FBI protection and his whereabouts have been described as unclear, which makes his availability at trial a live question rather than an assumption.

findings.claim: Twiggs' account supplies the most incriminating material in the case
findings.detail: By a wide margin. From his recorded statement and the exhibits drawn from his device: Robinson left home early on September 10, 2025 saying he had a long work shift, and there was no further contact until roughly 11 p.m., when Robinson directed him to look under a keyboard, where he found a handwritten note. He photographed it and replaced it. The following day he asked Robinson in person whether what he had said was true; by his account Robinson confirmed it, became briefly tearful, and said he wished he had not done it. Twiggs also said Robinson resembled the person on the FBI wanted poster, and that Robinson had been engraving bullets during 2025 while describing an upcoming family camping trip. Prosecutors noted he complied voluntarily with detectives and provided a DNA sample.

findings.claim: Twiggs was cross-examined about any of this
findings.detail: He was not, and this is the central structural problem. The state entered his sworn recorded account under Utah Rule 1102 as a recorded statement rather than calling him to the stand. The defence moved specifically to compel his live appearance, arguing he is “central” to the state's case and that the conversations between the two men are the asserted basis for seeking the death penalty. Prosecutors opposed, contending he was not material to a preliminary hearing given its light burden of proof. Judge Graf admitted most of the recorded interview over hearsay objection, ruling that the detectives' own statements in the video were admissible only to provide context for Twiggs' answers. The Confrontation Clause objection is preserved, so the question is deferred to trial rather than resolved.

findings.claim: Twiggs gave his account without legal exposure or incentive
findings.detail: He gave it under limited use immunity from both the United States Attorney's Office and the Utah County Attorney's Office, in a recorded sworn statement on April 20, 2026, after an admonition that false statements were punishable and could themselves be charged as obstruction. That structure cuts in two directions and both should be stated. It protects him from having his own words used against him, which removes one motive to shade an account, and the obstruction warning creates a direct penalty for fabrication. But immunity is granted to people who have some exposure to protect, and a witness who understands that his protection is conditional on the prosecution's satisfaction is not a disinterested one. None of this indicates he lied; it means his account was given inside an incentive structure a jury is entitled to weigh, and no cross-examiner has yet probed it.

findings.claim: Twiggs is the sole custodian of the note evidence
findings.detail: He found it, read it, photographed it, and replaced it under the keyboard. The physical original was subsequently destroyed — reported as partially burned — so his photograph is the evidentiary artefact. No handwriting comparison against a verified exemplar of Robinson's writing has been reported, and the note is quoted in mainstream reporting in two tenses that carry opposite meanings, a completed act versus a stated intention (see contradiction X21). A single uncross-examined witness being the entire chain of custody for the case's most quoted document is a genuine evidentiary weakness independent of whether his account is accurate.

findings.claim: The text thread reached the court through independent forensic authentication
findings.detail: It reached the court through Twiggs' device and was read into the record by an investigator. No digital-forensics witness testified to metadata, device-to-account linkage, or message-level timestamp verification. The exhibit photographs show a phone being held in someone's hand and displayed, not a forensic extraction report. This does not suggest the messages are fabricated — their operational content aligns closely with physical evidence recovered independently, which is itself a meaningful form of corroboration — but the authentication the public assumes has occurred has not been demonstrated on the record.

findings.claim: Twiggs' DNA on the key exhibits indicates involvement
findings.detail: The proportions argue strongly against it. FBI analyst Amanda Bakker testified to two-person mixtures with Robinson as the dominant contributor and Twiggs as the minor one on both items: roughly 95% Robinson to 5% Twiggs on the towel, and roughly 89% to 11% on the screwdriver. Trace-level minor contribution from a cohabiting partner on a household towel and a common tool is exactly what secondary transfer predicts. Several outlets nonetheless ran headlines foregrounding Twiggs' DNA, which inverts the emphasis of the testimony. What remains genuinely open is that no source reviewed contains an explicit on-record explanation of why his DNA is on these specific items — the innocent explanation is likely but was never actually put on the record.

findings.claim: Theories that Twiggs was more deeply involved have evidentiary support
findings.detail: Such theories circulate, including a dedicated page in the CharlieFiles material this app already catalogues. Nothing located supports them. He was not charged; both federal and county prosecutors extended immunity rather than pursuing him; authorities stated there is no indication he had prior knowledge; his DNA contribution is trace-level and consistent with cohabitation; and his account is against Robinson's interest rather than self-serving in any obvious way. The state's decision not to charge the one person who indisputably knew before the surrender is meaningful evidence that investigators found no wider circle. Recorded as not established rather than refuted only because his account has never been tested by cross-examination, which is the process that would ordinarily settle it.

findings.claim: Twiggs' availability for trial is assured
findings.detail: Reporting indicates he is no longer under FBI protection, and at least one outlet has described his whereabouts as unclear. Combined with the fact that he has never been cross-examined and that the defence's Confrontation objection is preserved, this is a live risk to the state's case rather than a formality. If a witness whose recorded statement carried this much weight proves unavailable at trial, the admissibility of that recording becomes a substantially harder question than it was at a probable-cause hearing, where the burden is light and hearsay is permitted. This app has not verified his current status beyond these reports.

findings.claim: Claims of internal inconsistency in Twiggs' timeline have been substantiated
findings.detail: Independent commentary asserting timeline problems in his account exists, but the sourcing located is self-published analysis rather than reporting from the courtroom or comparison against a transcript. This app has not obtained a transcript of the recorded interview and cannot test the claim. It is logged as unverified rather than dismissed, and it is precisely the category of question that cross-examination exists to resolve — which has not happened.

timeline_sequence.event: Twiggs meets Robinson; they begin a relationship two to three months after Robinson moves in
Twiggs observes Robinson engraving bullets; Robinson describes an upcoming family camping trip
Robinson leaves home saying he has a long work shift
First contact of the day: Robinson directs Twiggs to look under his keyboard; Twiggs finds, reads, photographs and replaces a handwritten note
Extended text exchange covering the rifle in a bush, fingerprint concerns, the engraved rounds, and a request to delete the exchange
Twiggs asks Robinson in person whether it was true; by his account Robinson confirms, becomes briefly tearful, says he wishes he had not done it. Twiggs leaves for his parents' home
Twiggs gives a recorded sworn statement under limited use immunity from both federal and county prosecutors, admonished that false statements are chargeable as obstruction
Defence moves to compel his live appearance for cross-examination; prosecutors argue he is not material; Judge Graf admits the recorded statement under Rule 1102 with redactions
The recorded interview is played on day four of the preliminary hearing over defence objection. Twiggs never appears in person

fact_check_gap: Coverage split into two incompatible distortions and neither matched the record. Headline treatments foregrounded Twiggs' DNA on the exhibits in a way that inverted testimony establishing him as the trace-level minor contributor, while other coverage treated his recorded account as though it were tested testimony. The genuinely important fact — that the witness whose conversations underpin a capital prosecution has never been cross-examined by anyone, over an explicit defence motion, on the prosecution's argument that he was not material — received comparatively little attention.

title: Site Geometry from Open-Source Imagery: The Venue Is a Sunken Terraced Amphitheatre
summary: An independent geospatial check of the shot geometry using OpenStreetMap building coordinates and aerial and oblique imagery of the UVU courtyard. Two results. The measured campus layout supports the 142-yard figure and argues strongly against 200 yards. And the venue turns out not to be a flat open space at all — it is a sunken, terraced amphitheatre, which reconciles an elevation figure that otherwise looked too large for the building, and which bears directly on the live dispute over whether the bullet passed above or through the crowd.
sources_quality: A for the coordinates (OpenStreetMap, ODbL, independently queryable); B for the distance comparison, which uses building centroids rather than the firing and stage positions; C+ for the height and terrace estimates, which are read off commercial oblique imagery with scale bars rather than surveyed
key_takeaway: Measured from OpenStreetMap, the Losee Center and Sorensen Student Center centroids are 112 m apart, about 122 yards. The reported hearing figures of 80 ft elevation and a 10.65° downward angle imply a horizontal distance of 129.7 m, or 141.8 yards — within about 18 m of the measured building separation, which is well inside the margin created by using centroids instead of actual firing and stage points. The 200-yard figure is a different matter: it would place the firing position roughly 71 m beyond the far side of the Sorensen centroid, and the imagery shows the courtyard is enclosed by buildings on multiple sides, so there is no obvious position at that range with line of sight into the space. Independent site data therefore supports 142 yards and undercuts 200. The second result is the more useful one. The imagery shows the event space is a stepped, sunken courtyard amphitheatre, with terraced lawn levels descending toward a central water feature. That matters twice over: a roof of ordinary academic height, roughly 55-65 ft above its own grade, sitting above a courtyard floor sunk 10-18 ft below that grade, produces a total drop of about 65-83 ft — which brackets the reported 80 ft without requiring the six- or seven-storey building that figure would otherwise imply. And because the terraces descend toward the stage, crowd members standing farther from the stage stood higher than those near it, which is a materially different geometry from the flat crowd both sides in the aggravator dispute appear to be assuming.

findings.claim: The 142-yard figure is consistent with the actual campus layout
findings.detail: OpenStreetMap places the Losee Center centroid at 40.27842, -111.71276 and the Sorensen Student Center centroid at 40.27859, -111.71406, a separation of 112.0 m or 122.5 yards. The hearing-derived figures of 80 ft elevation and a 10.65° angle independently imply 129.7 m, or 141.8 yards. The roughly 18 m difference is comfortably within the error introduced by using building centroids in place of the actual rooftop firing position and the actual stage position, each of which could sit tens of metres from its building's centre. Two independent methods — reported instrument figures and open geospatial data — converge on the same approximate distance.

findings.claim: The 200-yard figure is compatible with the site
findings.detail: At 200 yards the horizontal distance is 182.9 m, which would place the firing position about 71 m beyond the far side of the Sorensen Student Center centroid — not merely at the far edge of the Losee Center but well past the entire courtyard complex. The imagery shows the event space enclosed by buildings on multiple sides, including Sorensen to the northwest, the Environmental Technology Building to the west, and the Office of Admissions to the southeast. There is no evident position at that range with an unobstructed line of sight into the courtyard. Combined with the trigonometric incompatibility already logged — 80 ft at 200 yards requires a 7.59° angle, not 10.65° — the 200-yard figure appears to be a reporting error rather than a competing measurement.

findings.claim: The 80 ft elevation figure requires an unusually tall building
findings.detail: It does not, once the courtyard's sunken profile is accounted for, and this resolves a discrepancy this app had not previously noticed. Oblique imagery shows the surrounding academic buildings at roughly three to four storeys, which for buildings of this type is on the order of 45-65 ft above their own grade — short of 80 ft. But the courtyard is not at that grade. It is a stepped amphitheatre whose terraced lawn levels descend toward a central water feature, plausibly 10-18 ft below the surrounding plaza. A 55-65 ft roof above a courtyard floor sunk 10-18 ft yields a total vertical drop of roughly 65-83 ft, which brackets the reported figure. The 80 ft is therefore best read as roof-to-target elevation difference rather than building height, and it is internally consistent with the site. Heights here are estimated from imagery, not surveyed.

findings.claim: The crowd occupied a flat plane, as both sides in the aggravator dispute appear to assume
findings.detail: This is the finding with the most bearing on live litigation and it appears in no filing or coverage reviewed. The venue is a terraced amphitheatre in which the ground descends in discrete steps toward the stage area. Attendees therefore did not stand at a uniform elevation: those farther from the stage stood on higher terraces than those close to it. The defence contends the bullet “traveled above, not through, the crowd”; the prosecution contends bystanders sat inside a zone of danger. Both arguments are being made as though crowd head-height were a single constant, when the site geometry makes it a function of distance from the stage. On terrain that rises away from the target, a descending shot fired from beyond the crowd has less vertical clearance over distant attendees than a flat-ground model predicts, and more over those near the stage. Whether that helps or harms either party depends on measurements neither side has produced, which is precisely the point: the trajectory question cannot be settled on a flat-plane assumption, and no scene-specific reconstruction exists in the public record.

findings.claim: This imagery can establish the firing position, stage position, or a definitive trajectory
findings.detail: It cannot, and the limits should be stated plainly. Commercial aerial and oblique imagery with scale bars supports approximate distance and relative-height reasoning, not survey-grade measurement. The exact rooftop firing position is unknown beyond reporting placing prints near the northeast edge of the Losee Center; the exact stage and lectern position within the courtyard is not established in any source reviewed; and building heights here are inferred from storey counts rather than measured. The imagery is also dated 2026, and this app separately documents that the courtyard was altered with concrete pavers within days of the shooting under an emergency no-bid contract, so present-day imagery may not depict the September 2025 surface condition. Everything above is a plausibility bound. A genuine trajectory reconstruction would require the scene measurements, the autopsy wound track, and the stage layout together.

route_math.available_window: Implied by 80 ft at 10.65°: 129.7 m / 141.8 yards
route_math.shortfall: Difference between measured and implied: ~18 m, well within centroid-versus-actual-position error. The 200-yard scenario (182.9 m) would require a firing point ~71 m beyond the far side of the Sorensen centroid, with no evident line of sight into an enclosed courtyard.
route_math.note: Elevation reconciliation: a 55-65 ft roof above a courtyard floor sunk 10-18 ft below plaza grade yields a 65-83 ft drop, bracketing the reported 80 ft without requiring an unusually tall building.

fact_check_gap: The venue's terraced, sunken profile is visible in any public aerial view of the campus and appears in no filing, expert report, or news analysis reviewed for this app — despite a death-penalty aggravator turning on whether a bullet passed above or through the people standing in it. Both parties are litigating crowd exposure on an implicit flat-ground model that the site plainly contradicts.
